title: General practice: a brief vague question about diabetes group visits becomes a randomised comparison, not a records study of attenders
notes: Ordinary ambiguity from a brief, vague request (40 words; the input class admitted by amendment A3.2 section 3; the validator's lower bound of 120 words is being lowered to 20, so a need-word failure here is expected until then). The need names no design and no cue, so routing is unresolved at create; the problem reply omits family and constraints (omitKeys), listing the missing facts as unknowns, so the family stays unset and the empty constraints stay empty (G11: nothing typed, nothing invented). A fixture search returns six records; the appraisal records four claims, including one showing that attenders differ from non-attenders. The Design stage faces two candidate designs, the records comparison the practice could run now and a randomised comparison, and refuses the first as confounded; it recommends rct. The proposed recommendation must not set the family (D3 within S11); acceptance sets it with basis 'explicit'. Both gates (neighbouring practices joining, ethics approval and registration) are unknown, so the accepted decision stays blocked. The study is reopened right after acceptance. Requires S13 (appraisal dispatch), S11 (routing, recommendedFamily, selectionStatus, actionStatus, family on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text). Catches: a guessed family or invented constraints for a vague request, a family set by a proposal, and a confounded comparison accepted as an answer.

records.title: Group medical visits for adults with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Adeyinka-Solberg M, Fairbairn-Otieno C, Leclerc-Mahmoud S
records.abstract: We included 26 randomised trials (4,410 adults) comparing group medical visits, in which a clinician sees 6 to 15 patients together for education and individual review, with usual individual care for type 2 diabetes. At 6 to 12 months, group visits lowered HbA1c by a mean of 4.4 mmol/mol (95 percent CI 2.7 to 6.1), with no clear effect on blood pressure or weight. Heterogeneity was substantial, and effects were larger in trials with more sessions and higher baseline HbA1c. Only eight trials reported patient-reported outcomes, and attendance was reported inconsistently.

records.title: Group consultations versus usual care for type 2 diabetes in general practice: a cluster-randomised trial in 24 practices
records.authors: Mortensen-Achebe L, Dubois-Nakamura T, Okafor-Lindqvist J
records.abstract: Twenty-four practices were randomly allocated to offer group consultations or usual individual reviews to adults with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol or more. At 12 months the mean difference in HbA1c was 2.1 mmol/mol in favour of group consultations (95 percent CI -0.6 to 4.8), and diabetes distress scores improved more in the group arm. Only 61 percent of invited patients attended at least half the sessions. Nurse time per patient was 35 percent lower, but patients who worked full time attended least.

records.title: Outcomes of patients attending diabetes group visits compared with non-attenders: a retrospective records study
records.abstract: Using records from four practices, we compared 412 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended group visits with 1,630 who did not. Attenders had a 6 mmol/mol lower HbA1c after a year, but they were younger, more often retired and had better HbA1c before their first group visit. After adjustment for age and baseline HbA1c, the difference fell to 2 mmol/mol. The authors note that motivation, which the records do not capture, probably explains part of the remaining difference, and they recommend a randomised comparison.

records.title: Company, comparison and privacy: patients' experiences of diabetes group visits
records.abstract: We interviewed 31 adults with type 2 diabetes who had been offered group visits in three practices. Many valued meeting others with the same condition and learning from their experiences. Some felt uncomfortable discussing weight or results in front of neighbours and preferred individual reviews. People who spoke limited English and people with shift work found it hardest to take part. Participants suggested short individual time within each session and evening options. Interviews were conducted by practice staff, which may have limited criticism, and nobody who had declined the offer outright was interviewed.

records.title: Clinician time and costs of group visits for type 2 diabetes in primary care: a cost analysis
records.abstract: We costed group visits in six practices over one year using staff diaries and appointment records. Each 90-minute session for about ten patients used a nurse and a GP for part of the session. Clinician time per patient was 28 percent lower than for equivalent individual reviews, but administrative time for booking and reminders was higher. Savings depended on sessions being at least 70 percent full. The analysis did not include patient time or travel costs. Sessions that were less than half full cost more per patient than individual reviews.

records.title: Contamination in individually randomised trials of group-based care in general practice: a methods study
records.abstract: We examined 18 individually randomised trials of group-based interventions delivered in general practice. In nine, the same clinicians delivered both arms, and six reported changes in usual care during the trial that could dilute the comparison. Clustering within groups in the intervention arm was ignored in 11 trials, which overstated precision. We recommend partially nested analyses, separating clinicians where feasible, and reporting what usual care looked like during the trial. Only four trials described usual care during the trial period, and none measured whether patients in the comparison arm heard about the groups from other patients.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Trials overall suggest group visits lower HbA1c modestly, but the most applicable general practice trial found a small effect with an interval crossing zero and incomplete attendance. Comparisons of attenders with non-attenders are confounded by who chooses to attend. Group visits may save clinician time when sessions are full, but patients with limited English or shift work take part least. Individually randomised trials of group care need partially nested analyses and attention to shared clinicians.
response.gradeRationale: Many randomised trials with a consistent direction for HbA1c, downgraded once for inconsistency; the applicable general practice trial is imprecise.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty moderate for HbA1c.

response.overview: Individually randomised trial of group medical visits against usual individual reviews for adults with type 2 diabetes above target, across the practice and neighbouring practices, with partial nesting of groups in the intervention arm.
response.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes and HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol or more in the last six months, able to consent; excluded are people receiving palliative care or already in a structured education programme.
response.exposure: Intervention: six 90-minute group visits over 12 months for 8 to 12 patients, led by a practice nurse with a GP for part of each session, including short individual time. Comparator: usual individual reviews at the practice's usual frequency.
response.procedures: Eligible patients are identified from records and invited by letter; consenting patients are randomised 1:1 by a remote web system, stratified by practice and baseline HbA1c. Where possible, different nurses deliver group and individual care. HbA1c is measured at baseline and 12 months in routine blood tests; questionnaires are completed at baseline and 12 months.

response.summary: Partially nested individually randomised trial with HbA1c as the primary outcome.

response.designSummary: Individually randomised, partially nested trial comparing group visits with individual reviews.
response.sampleSize: To detect a 4 mmol/mol difference in HbA1c with a standard deviation of 14, 80 percent power and two-sided alpha 0.05 needs 193 patients per arm. Groups of about 10 with an intracluster correlation of 0.03 give the intervention arm a design effect of about 1.27; applying it to both arms for simplicity gives about 245 per arm; allowing 15 percent loss to follow-up gives about 290 per arm, 580 in total. This exceeds what one practice is likely to have, so neighbouring practices are needed.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear mixed model for 12-month HbA1c with arm, baseline HbA1c and practice as fixed effects and a random effect for group in the intervention arm only (partially nested), by intention to treat.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model for diabetes distress; attendance described by age, work status and language; hypoglycaemia episodes compared descriptively.
response.missingData: Multiple imputation under missing at random using baseline HbA1c, practice and arm; a sensitivity analysis with a pattern-mixture approach.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes reported with confidence intervals.
response.software: R with the lme4 package; analysis plan finalised before unblinding.
overfittingGuards: Adjustment limited to stratification variables and baseline HbA1c
Analysis plan fixed before data lock
response.summary: About 580 patients for 80 percent power to detect 4 mmol/mol with partial nesting.

response.risks: Low: both arms receive active diabetes care; group visits may expose personal results to other patients.
response.consent: Written informed consent after an information sheet; group participants agree to keep other members' information confidential; patients can switch to individual reviews at any time.
response.data: Pseudonymised trial database held by the practice network's research team; routine laboratory results extracted with consent.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with limited English, shift work or caring duties attend least. Sessions are offered in the evening with interpreting, and attendance and outcomes are reported by age, work status and language.
response.effectiveness: The trial tells the partners whether expansion is worth it.
response.efficiency: Group visits may save clinician time if sessions are full; the trial records nurse time.
response.costs: Research nurse time for recruitment and data collection, not yet funded.
response.grants: A primary care research grant would be needed; none is in place.
response.partnerships: Neighbouring practices, the local diabetes specialist nurse team, and two patients with type 2 diabetes as advisers.
response.rebPath: Full research ethics review under ICH-GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki, and registration in a public trial registry before recruitment; neither has been started.
response.limitations: Unblinded delivery, possible contamination, and dependence on neighbouring practices joining.
response.summary: Low-risk trial with consent, confidentiality rules for groups and equity measures; funding, practices and approvals are not yet in place.

response.title: Group medical visits versus individual reviews for adults with type 2 diabetes in general practice: protocol for an individually randomised, partially nested trial
response.abstract: Objective: to compare HbA1c at 12 months between adults with type 2 diabetes offered group medical visits and those continuing individual reviews. Design: individually randomised, partially nested trial across several general practices. Participants: adults with HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol or more. Results will be reported after follow-up.
response.introduction: Group medical visits lower HbA1c modestly in trials, but a general practice trial was imprecise, and comparisons of attenders with non-attenders are confounded by self-selection.
response.methods: Consenting patients are randomised 1:1 by a remote system, stratified by practice and baseline HbA1c. The primary outcome is laboratory HbA1c at 12 months, analysed with a linear mixed model with a random effect for group in the intervention arm.
response.results: No patients have been recruited yet. The report will present recruitment, attendance, HbA1c and distress by arm, and hypoglycaemia.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the effect against the pooled estimate, attendance and equity, and state what the result means for expanding group visits.
response.limitations: Unblinded delivery, possible contamination, and reliance on neighbouring practices for recruitment.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial.
response.reportingChecklist: SPIRIT 2013 for the protocol; CONSORT 2010 with the non-pharmacological extension for the results
